title: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection: Pain Out of Proportion Is an Emergency Cue
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Rapidly progressive pain, swelling, systemic toxicity, bullae, dusky skin, crepitus, or pain out of proportion to visible findings can signal necrotizing infection. Escalate for urgent surgical evaluation; do not wait for dramatic skin necrosis.
recognize: Severe pain, rapidly spreading erythema, edema beyond visible margins, fever, hypotension, bullae, skin anesthesia, or crepitus.
priorities: Assess ABCs/perfusion, mark/track progression if ordered, activate urgent surgical/sepsis pathway, and prepare for IV therapy/operative management.
assessMonitor: Vital signs, mental status, pain, skin progression, urine output, lactate/labs as ordered, and organ dysfunction.
interventions: Support resuscitation and ordered antimicrobials; keep the patient NPO when surgery is likely.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics do not replace source control; broad-spectrum therapy is provider directed.
teaching: Seek urgent care for rapidly worsening pain/swelling or systemic illness after a wound or procedure.
delegationScope: Focused monitoring is appropriate; diagnosis, antimicrobial selection, and surgical decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Waiting for black skin before suspecting necrotizing infection.
oneLinePearl: Severe pain can precede dramatic skin findings.

title: Cellulitis Deterioration: Local Infection Can Become Systemic
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Cellulitis with rapidly expanding redness, severe pain, fever, hypotension, altered mental status, or organ dysfunction requires escalation for invasive infection/sepsis evaluation.
recognize: Increasing erythema/warmth/swelling, lymphangitic spread, fever, drainage, or systemic symptoms.
priorities: Assess progression and systemic stability and notify the provider promptly when deterioration is present.
assessMonitor: Vital signs, skin margins, pain, drainage, hydration, glucose in diabetes, and response to therapy.
interventions: Elevate affected limb when appropriate, protect skin, administer ordered antimicrobials, and reassess response.
medicationSafety: Do not change antibiotics independently because redness persists early in therapy; worsening systemic status requires clinical reassessment.
teaching: Complete prescribed therapy and seek care for spreading redness, fever, severe pain, or weakness.
delegationScope: Routine measurements may be delegated; deterioration interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Focusing only on the skin margin while missing hypotension and confusion.
oneLinePearl: Cellulitis becomes urgent when the patient—not just the skin—looks worse.
sourceBasis: CDC Group A Streptococcus clinical guidance

title: Diabetic Foot Infection: Neuropathy Can Hide Serious Tissue Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A diabetic foot wound can be severe despite limited pain because neuropathy masks injury. Drainage, malodor, spreading erythema, deep tissue exposure, systemic illness, or ischemic change requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: Ulcer depth, drainage, erythema, warmth, swelling, tissue discoloration, reduced sensation, and poor perfusion.
priorities: Assess wound and neurovascular status, offload/protect the area, and escalate infection or ischemia cues.
assessMonitor: Wound dimensions, drainage, temperature, glucose, pulses/perfusion, sensation, and ordered imaging/labs.
interventions: Use prescribed wound care/offloading and antimicrobial plan; involve foot/wound specialists as indicated.
medicationSafety: Topical products and antibiotics should follow the wound diagnosis and treatment plan.
teaching: Inspect feet daily and avoid walking barefoot or self-cutting calluses.
delegationScope: Routine wound care may be assigned by policy; infection/perfusion changes require licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Using lack of pain to rule out serious diabetic foot infection.
oneLinePearl: Neuropathy can mute pain while tissue damage progresses.

title: Pressure Injury Infection: Watch Beyond the Wound Surface
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pressure injuries can progress to deep infection or osteomyelitis. New purulence, foul drainage, surrounding cellulitis, exposed bone, fever, or unexplained deterioration warrants escalation.
recognize: Increasing drainage, odor, friable tissue, warmth, erythema, undermining, exposed structures, or systemic decline.
priorities: Relieve pressure, assess wound/systemic status, and communicate infection concerns promptly.
assessMonitor: Wound size/depth, drainage, surrounding skin, pain, nutrition, mobility, temperature, and labs/imaging as ordered.
interventions: Use pressure redistribution, moisture management, nutrition support, and prescribed wound care.
medicationSafety: Do not use topical/systemic antimicrobials solely for odor without clinical evaluation of infection.
teaching: Reposition and protect skin according to individualized prevention plan.
delegationScope: Repositioning and routine skin care may be delegated; wound deterioration requires licensed review.
examTrap: Assuming a chronic wound cannot be the source of acute systemic decline.
oneLinePearl: Pressure injury depth and infection can exceed what is visible at the surface.

title: Animal or Human Bite: Infection and Tetanus Risk Need Review
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Bites can inoculate deep tissue and may require infection prophylaxis/treatment, tetanus assessment, and selected rabies evaluation. Hand, face, deep puncture, immunocompromised, or infected wounds deserve prompt review.
recognize: Puncture wounds, crush injury, tendon/joint involvement, erythema, swelling, drainage, fever, or uncertain animal status.
priorities: Clean the wound, assess depth/function/neurovascular status, review tetanus history, and notify the provider for antimicrobial/rabies decisions.
assessMonitor: Pain, range of motion, drainage, systemic symptoms, and wound progression.
interventions: Irrigate/clean according to protocol and protect the wound.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics do not substitute for tetanus vaccination/TIG decisions; rabies prophylaxis is exposure-specific.
teaching: Seek care for deep bites and keep tetanus vaccination current.
delegationScope: Basic wound cleansing may be performed by trained staff; prophylaxis decisions are provider/public-health directed.
oneLinePearl: Bite care requires wound, tetanus, infection, and sometimes rabies assessment.

title: Puncture Wound: Small Opening Can Hide Deep Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A puncture wound can carry contamination deep into tissue despite a small surface opening. Assess retained foreign body, neurovascular status, infection risk, and tetanus prophylaxis needs.
recognize: Deep penetration, footwear-associated plantar puncture, dirty object, retained fragment, worsening pain, swelling, drainage, or fever.
priorities: Clean the wound, assess function/perfusion/sensation, review immunization history, and escalate deep or infected wounds.
assessMonitor: Pain, swelling, drainage, range of motion, neurovascular findings, and systemic symptoms.
interventions: Remove superficial debris only as appropriate; deeper foreign-body management is provider directed.
medicationSafety: Routine antibiotics solely to prevent tetanus are not indicated; infection treatment is scenario-specific.
teaching: Report worsening pain, swelling, drainage, fever, or reduced function.
delegationScope: Basic wound care may be shared; deep injury evaluation requires licensed/provider assessment.
examTrap: Judging puncture severity by surface size alone.
oneLinePearl: Tiny entrance wounds can conceal major depth.

title: Water-Exposed Wound: Rapid Pain or Bullae Need Urgent Escalation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Open wounds exposed to natural water can develop severe infection, particularly in people with liver disease or immune compromise. Rapid pain, swelling, bullae, skin discoloration, fever, or shock requires emergency evaluation.
recognize: Recent seawater/brackish-water exposure, wound contamination, chronic liver disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise.
priorities: Assess systemic status and wound progression and notify the provider promptly.
assessMonitor: Vital signs, pain, skin changes, bullae, drainage, and organ dysfunction.
interventions: Clean/protect wounds and avoid further water exposure until healed as advised.
medicationSafety: Antimicrobial selection depends on organism/exposure and is provider directed.
teaching: Avoid natural-water exposure with open wounds, especially if medically high risk.
delegationScope: Monitoring is appropriate; antimicrobial/surgical decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Treating rapidly progressive water-exposed wound pain as simple cellulitis without escalation.
oneLinePearl: Water exposure plus rapid tissue change can signal invasive infection.
sourceBasis: CDC Group A Strep wound prevention guidance 2026

title: Skin Abscess: Source Control May Matter More Than More Antibiotic
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: A fluctuant purulent collection may require drainage/source control. Repeated antibiotics without evaluation of a drainable abscess can delay recovery.
recognize: Localized fluctuance, focal tenderness, purulent drainage, surrounding erythema, fever, or recurrent lesions.
priorities: Assess size/location/systemic status and notify the provider when drainage or culture is indicated.
assessMonitor: Pain, erythema, drainage, fever, recurrence, and response after treatment.
interventions: Use prescribed wound care and contact precautions when indicated; do not squeeze deep abscesses.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic need depends on severity, systemic features, host risk, and drainage status.
teaching: Do not share towels/razors and keep draining wounds covered as instructed.
delegationScope: Routine wound care may be delegated; incision/drainage and treatment selection are provider/credential dependent.
examTrap: Assuming every abscess is solved by changing antibiotics.
oneLinePearl: Pus often needs source control, not just another prescription.

title: Dirty or Major Wound: Tetanus Protection Depends on Wound Type and Vaccine History
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Tetanus prevention requires wound cleaning plus vaccination-history review, with TIG only for specific higher-risk situations. Antibiotics are not used solely to prevent tetanus.
recognize: Puncture, bite, crush, burn, compound fracture, frostbite, necrotic, or contaminated wounds carry higher tetanus risk.
priorities: Clean/debride as ordered, verify primary-series and last-dose history, and follow CDC vaccine/TIG recommendations.
assessMonitor: Wound contamination, tissue viability, infection signs, and immunization documentation.
interventions: Administer indicated vaccine/TIG when ordered and monitor for reaction.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute antibiotics for vaccine/TIG decisions.
redFlags: Unknown vaccine history with dirty wound
teaching: Keep tetanus-containing vaccines current and bring immunization records when possible.
delegationScope: Vaccine administration follows policy; prophylaxis interpretation may require licensed/provider review.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics specifically to prevent tetanus.
oneLinePearl: Tetanus prevention is wound care plus immunization logic—not antibiotics.

title: Wound Deterioration: Trend Tissue, Drainage, Pain, and the Patient
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Wound evaluation is longitudinal. Increasing pain, drainage, malodor, tissue discoloration, size/depth, surrounding inflammation, fever, or functional decline requires reassessment of the treatment plan.
recognize: A wound that is larger, wetter, more painful, more necrotic, or associated with systemic symptoms is not improving.
priorities: Compare with prior findings and escalate clinically meaningful deterioration.
assessMonitor: Size/depth, tissue type, drainage, odor, surrounding skin, pain, perfusion, nutrition, glucose when relevant, and systemic status.
interventions: Continue ordered cleansing/dressing/offloading/pressure-relief plan and document objective trends.
medicationSafety: Avoid unapproved topical agents that obscure assessment or injure tissue.
teaching: Report increasing pain, drainage, redness, odor, fever, or black tissue.
delegationScope: Routine wound measurements may be assigned to trained staff; interpretation and plan changes require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Documenting the wound as unchanged without comparing objective measurements and patient condition.
oneLinePearl: A wound trend is a clinical outcome, not just a dressing task.
